Lower-face radial construction lines are retained. Nonsemantic source face shading is omitted under house style.

spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no calculated answers are shown.

solidReview.evidence: .booklet-work/solid-quality-20261028/batch/s6adv-applications-of-calculus-2-optimisation-v1/pages/feedback-pages.json; actual student PDF pages 53,54,55,63,64,65 and source geometry visually inspected; unchanged dimensions, labels and edition widths.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the cylinder has radius $r$ metres, show that $r^2=R^2-\frac14h^2$.

answer.worked:
The sphere centre is halfway up the cylinder. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}R^2&=\left(\frac h2\right)^2+r^2\\r^2&=R^2-\frac14h^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by $V=\frac\pi4h(4R^2-h^2)$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^2h\\V&=\pi\left(R^2-\frac14h^2\right)h\\V&=\frac\pi4h(4R^2-h^2).\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the cylinder is maximised when $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$.

answer.short: $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$. Since $\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\frac{3\pi h}{2}<0$ for $0<h<2R$, this gives the maximum.
answer.worked:
For a nondegenerate cylinder, $0<h<2R$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dV}{dh}&=\frac\pi4(4R^2-3h^2)\\0&=4R^2-3h^2\\h^2&=\frac{4R^2}{3}\\h&=\sqrt{\frac{4R^2}{3}}\\h&=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R.\end{align*}$$
The positive root is in the domain. Also,
$$\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\frac{6\pi h}{4}<0\qquad(h>0).$$
Thus $V$ is concave down throughout the domain, so its stationary point gives the global maximum.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence show that the ratio of the volume of the sphere to the maximum volume of the cylinder is $\sqrt3:1$.

answer.worked:
At the maximum, $h=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R$ and $h^2=\frac{4R^2}{3}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi r^2h}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi\left(R^2-\frac14h^2\right)\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\pi\left(R^2-\frac14\frac{4R^2}{3}\right)\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}R}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\frac{\frac43\pi R^3}{\frac{4\sqrt3}{9}\pi R^3}\\\frac{V_{\mathrm{sphere}}}{V_{\mathrm{cylinder,max}}}&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Therefore the required ratio is $\sqrt3:1$.

content.prompt: A rectangle has a constant area of $36\text{ cm}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If $x$ is the length of the rectangle, show that the width is $\dfrac{36}{x}$.

answer.worked:
Let $y$ be the width in centimetres, with $x>0$.
$$\begin{align*}xy&=36\\y&=\frac{36}{x}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the perimeter of the rectangle is given by $P=2x+\dfrac{72}{x}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}P&=2x+2y\\P&=2x+2\left(\frac{36}{x}\right)\\P&=2x+\frac{72}{x}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=2-\dfrac{72}{x^2}$ and hence that the minimum value of $P$ occurs at $x=6$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=2-\dfrac{72}{x^2}$. The derivative changes from negative to positive at $x=6$, so $P$ has its minimum there.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the minimum possible perimeter of the rectangle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(6)&=2(6)+\frac{72}{6}\\P(6)&=24\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
The minimum possible perimeter is $24\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: A 10 cm length of wire is cut into two pieces from which two squares are formed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If one piece has length $x$, find the side length of each square.

answer.worked:
Each side is one quarter of its square's perimeter.
$$\begin{align*}s_1&=\frac{x}{4}\text{ cm}\\s_2&=\frac{10-x}{4}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the combined area of the two squares is $A=\dfrac{x^2-10x+50}{8}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A&=\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{10-x}{4}\right)^2\\A&=\frac{2x^2-20x+100}{16}\\A&=\frac{x^2-10x+50}{8}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ and hence find the value of $x$ that minimises $A$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dA}{dx}&=\frac{2x-10}{8}\\\frac{dA}{dx}&=\frac{x-5}{4}\\\frac{x-5}{4}&=0\\x&=5.\end{align*}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac14>0$ for all $x$, the function is concave up. Thus $A$ is minimised at $x=5$ cm, within the physical domain $0<x<10$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the least possible combined area.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A(5)&=\frac{5^2-10(5)+50}{8}\\A(5)&=\frac{25}{8}\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$
The least possible combined area is $\dfrac{25}{8}\text{ cm}^2$.

content.prompt: A farmer has 480 m of fencing to build a rectangular enclosure divided into three pens by two internal fences, as shown. What are the dimensions of the enclosure that give the greatest total area?

answer.short: The internal fences are 60 m long and the enclosure is 120 m wide: 60 m by 120 m (greatest area $7200\text{ m}^2$).
answer.worked:
Let $x$ m be the length of each of the four fences running the same way as the internal fences, and $y$ m the length of each of the other two.
$$\begin{aligned}4x+2y&=480\\y&=240-2x\\A(x)&=x(240-2x)\\A(x)&=240x-2x^2,\qquad 0<x<120\\A'(x)&=240-4x.\end{aligned}$$
Setting $A'(x)=0$ gives $x=60$.
$$\begin{aligned}A''(x)&=-4<0\\y&=240-2(60)=120\\A(60)&=60(120)=7200.\end{aligned}$$
The quadratic opens downwards, so this is the global maximum. The enclosure should be 60 m by 120 m, giving a total area of $7200\text{ m}^2$.

content.prompt: The council wants to make a rectangular swimming area at the beach using the seashore on one side and 300 m of shark-proof netting for 3 sides. What are the dimensions of the rectangle that encloses the greatest area?

spec.description: Three unlabelled netted sides beneath a light blue shore strip extending beyond both vertical sides. The strip identifies the unnetted side.
spec.mathematics: A rectangular enclosure uses netting on two perpendicular widths and one length.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no dimensions or answers supplied.

answer.short: $150$ m along the seashore and $75$ m perpendicular to it; greatest area $11\,250\text{ m}^2$.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ m be each side perpendicular to the shore and $y$ m the side parallel to it.
$$\begin{aligned}2x+y&=300\\y&=300-2x\\A(x)&=x(300-2x)\\A(x)&=300x-2x^2,\qquad 0<x<150\\A'(x)&=300-4x.\end{aligned}$$
Setting $A'(x)=0$ gives $x=75$.
$$\begin{aligned}A''(x)&=-4<0\\y&=300-2(75)=150\\A(75)&=75(150)=11\,250.\end{aligned}$$
The quadratic opens downwards, so this is the global maximum. The dimensions are $150$ m along the shore and $75$ m perpendicular to it, giving an area of $11\,250\text{ m}^2$.

content.prompt:
$X$ is a point on the curve $y=x^2-2x+5$.

Point $Y$ lies directly below $X$ and is on the curve $y=4x-x^2$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 13, below the prompt on the left
spec.description: Two equation-driven parabolas with arrowheads, unticked Cartesian axes and a vertical segment joining X to Y to the left of the y-axis. Ordinary axes and labels use house black; the source blue curves and distance segment use standard blue. No shading.
spec.mathematics: Upper curve y=x^2-2x+5; lower curve y=4x-x^2. X and Y have the same x-coordinate. The illustrated coordinate is qualitative and is not a numerical given.
spec.answerVisibility: Visible in the question and answer editions.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the distance, $d$, between $X$ and $Y$ is $d=2x^2-6x+5$.

answer.worked:
Since $X$ and $Y$ have the same $x$-coordinate, subtract the lower ordinate from the upper ordinate:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=(x^2-2x+5)-(4x-x^2)\\d&=2x^2-6x+5.\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: Find the minimum distance between $X$ and $Y$.

content.prompt: Engineers have determined that the strength $s$ of a rectangular beam varies as the product of the width $w$ and the square of the depth $d$ of the beam, that is, $s=kwd^2$ for some $k>0$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 25, circular log cross-section below the parts
spec.description: Unshaded circle containing an inscribed rectangle. Its bottom-left to top-right diagonal passes through the marked centre and is labelled 48 cm. The bottom side is labelled w, the right side d, and the bottom-right corner has an internal right-angle mark. Ordinary source grey outlines use house black.
spec.mathematics: The rectangle's diagonal is a diameter of the circle, so w²+d²=48². The schematic aspect ratio supplies no additional measurement.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; optimised dimensions are not shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A particular cylindrical log has a diameter of 48 cm. Use Pythagoras' theorem to show that $s=kw(2304-w^2)$.

answer.worked:
By Pythagoras' theorem,
$$\begin{align*}w^2+d^2&=48^2\\d^2&=2304-w^2.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $s=kwd^2$, where $k>0$:
$$s=kw(2304-w^2).$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence find the dimensions of the strongest rectangular beam that can be cut from the log.

answer.worked:
For a non-degenerate beam, $0<w<48$.
$$\begin{align*}s&=2304kw-kw^3\\\frac{ds}{dw}&=2304k-3kw^2.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}2304k-3kw^2&=0\\w^2&=768\\w&=16\sqrt3\qquad(w>0).\end{align*}$$
Also,
$$\frac{d^2s}{dw^2}=-6kw.$$
Since $k>0$, $\dfrac{d^2s}{dw^2}<0$ throughout $0<w<48$. Thus strength is maximised at $w=16\sqrt3\text{ cm}$.

Substitute into $d^2=2304-w^2$:
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=2304-(16\sqrt3)^2\\d^2&=1536\\d&=16\sqrt6\qquad(d>0).\end{align*}$$
The dimensions are width $16\sqrt3\text{ cm}$ and depth $16\sqrt6\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt:
A cylinder $h$ cm high with radius $r$ cm is enclosed in a cone of height $40$ cm and radius $12$ cm.

The cylinder stands on the cone’s base and shares its axis. The diagram shows half of an axial cross-section: $A$ is the apex; $D$ is the base centre; $E$ is on the cone’s base rim; $B$ is on the axis at the cylinder’s top; and $C$ is its contact point with the cone.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle ADE$.

answer.short: AA similarity: $\angle ABC=\angle ADE=90^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=\angle AED$.
answer.worked: $\angle ABC=\angle ADE=90^\circ$. Also, $\angle ACB=\angle AED$ because $BC\parallel DE$ and $A,C,E$ lie on a straight line. Therefore $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle ADE$ by AA similarity.

children.label: b
children.prompt: By using ratios of corresponding sides, show that $h=40-\dfrac{10r}{3}$.

answer.worked:
Since $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle ADE$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BC}{DE}&=\frac{AB}{AD}\\\frac{r}{12}&=\frac{40-h}{40}\\\frac{40r}{12}&=40-h\\h&=40-\frac{10r}{3}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by $V=40\pi r^2-\dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^2h\\V&=\pi r^2\left(40-\frac{10r}{3}\right)\\V&=40\pi r^2-\frac{10\pi r^3}{3}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find $\dfrac{dV}{dr}$ and hence find the value of $r$ for which the volume of the cylinder is maximised.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=80\pi r-10\pi r^2=10\pi r(8-r)$. The volume is maximised when $r=8\,\mathrm{cm}$.
answer.worked:
For a non-degenerate cylinder, $0<r<12$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dV}{dr}&=80\pi r-10\pi r^2\\\frac{dV}{dr}&=10\pi r(8-r).\end{align*}$$
The derivative is zero when $r=0$ or $r=8$; only $r=8$ is in the domain.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2V}{dr^2}&=80\pi-20\pi r\\\left.\frac{d^2V}{dr^2}\right|_{r=8}&=-80\pi<0.\end{align*}$$
Also, $dV/dr>0$ for $0<r<8$ and $dV/dr<0$ for $8<r<12$, so this is the global maximum. The required radius is $8\,\mathrm{cm}$.

content.prompt: Prove that for all rectangles with a fixed perimeter, the one with the greatest area is a square.

answer.short: For fixed perimeter $k>0$, the maximum area occurs when $x=y=\dfrac{k}{4}$. Therefore the rectangle is a square.
answer.worked:
Let the fixed perimeter be $k>0$ and the side lengths be $x$ and $y$.
$$\begin{align*}k&=2x+2y\\y&=\frac{k-2x}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The domain is $0<x<\dfrac{k}{2}$.
$$\begin{align*}A(x)&=x\left(\frac{k-2x}{2}\right)\\A(x)&=\frac{kx}{2}-x^2\\A'(x)&=\frac{k}{2}-2x.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{k}{2}-2x&=0\\x&=\frac{k}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Since $A''(x)=-2<0$ throughout the domain, this gives the global maximum area.
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{k-2(k/4)}{2}\\y&=\frac{k}{4}.\end{align*}$$
The length and width are equal and each is a quarter of the perimeter. Therefore the rectangle with the greatest area is a square.

content.prompt: The sum of the radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ of two circles is such that $r_1+r_2=k$, where $k$ is a constant.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find an expression for the sum $S$ of the areas of the circles in terms of $r_1$.

answer.worked:
$r_1+r_2=k$, so $r_2=k-r_1$.
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi r_1^2+\pi r_2^2\\S&=\pi r_1^2+\pi(k-r_1)^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence show that the sum of the areas is least when $r_1=r_2$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dS}{dr_1}=0$ when $r_1=r_2$, and $\dfrac{d^2S}{dr_1^2}=4\pi>0$, so the sum of the areas is least when $r_1=r_2$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dS}{dr_1}&=2\pi r_1-2\pi(k-r_1)\\\frac{dS}{dr_1}&=2\pi(r_1-r_2)\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}2\pi(r_1-r_2)&=0\\r_1&=r_2.\end{align*}$$
Also,
$$\frac{d^2S}{dr_1^2}=4\pi>0.$$
The second derivative is positive throughout the domain $0<r_1<k$, so this stationary point is the global minimum. Thus the sum of the areas is least when $r_1=r_2$.

content.prompt: The rectangle PQRS has two vertices on the $x$-axis and two on the curve $y=e^{-x^2}$, as shown in the diagram. Find:

spec.description: Symmetric exponential curve with a rectangle beneath it, upper-right vertex P, lower-right Q, lower-left R and upper-left S. Both axes have arrowheads and no numbered ticks. The origin label is omitted under the house graph convention.
spec.mathematics: The curve is y=exp(-x^2). The illustrative rectangle has upper corners at opposite horizontal coordinates and equal positive heights; its width is 2x and height exp(-x^2). The illustrative coordinate used to draw it is not a given.
spec.answerVisibility: All givens and vertex labels remain visible in the question edition. No optimum is marked. Light blue shading identifies the assessed area, replacing source grey under the standard palette; source image hash 6e17ccf8b15ca2c8bbb1ae8c0f1c8a4e38cedd1d97f3526092e3ee66ba877dee.

children.label: a
children.prompt: the value of $x$ for which the rectangle has a maximum area

answer.worked:
The curve is even, so $S=(-x,e^{-x^2})$. Since P is the upper-right vertex, $x>0$.

Width $=2x$ and height $=e^{-x^2}$.
$$\begin{align*}A(x)&=2xe^{-x^2}\\A'(x)&=2e^{-x^2}-4x^2e^{-x^2}\\A'(x)&=2e^{-x^2}(1-2x^2).\end{align*}$$
For a stationary point, $e^{-x^2}>0$, so
$$\begin{align*}1-2x^2&=0\\x^2&=\frac12\\x&=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\qquad(x>0).\end{align*}$$
For $0<x<1/\sqrt2$, $A'(x)>0$; for $x>1/\sqrt2$, $A'(x)<0$. Thus the area increases then decreases throughout its domain, giving a global maximum at $x=\sqrt2/2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: the maximum area of the rectangle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)&=2\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)e^{-(\sqrt2/2)^2}\\A\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)&=\sqrt2\,e^{-1/2}\\A\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)&=\sqrt{\frac2e}.\end{align*}$$
The maximum area is $\sqrt{2/e}$ square units.

spec.sourceRegion: Cylinder below question 20 on the left
spec.description: Upright closed cylinder with an elliptical top, visible curved lower rim, a centre-to-right-rim radius arrow labelled r and an external vertical height arrow labelled h. Non-mathematical grey shading is omitted.

spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied figure; no solution information.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the height of the can is $\frac{250}{\pi r^2}$, where $r$ is the base radius.

answer.worked:
Let the height of the can be $h$ cm. The volume is $\pi r^2h$.
$$\begin{align*}250&=\pi r^2h\\h&=\frac{250}{\pi r^2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the total surface area is $S=2\pi r^2+\frac{500}{r}$.

answer.worked:
Each end has area $\pi r^2$ and the curved side has area $2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\S&=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\times\frac{250}{\pi r^2}\\S&=2\pi r^2+\frac{500}{r},\qquad r>0.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $r=\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}$ gives a global minimum of $S$ in the domain $r>0$.

answer.short: $r=\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}$ is stationary and $\frac{d^2S}{dr^2}=4\pi+\frac{1000}{r^3}>0$ for every $r>0$, so it gives the global minimum.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dS}{dr}&=4\pi r-\frac{500}{r^2}\\\frac{dS}{dr}&=\frac{4\pi r^3-500}{r^2}.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dS}{dr}&=0\\4\pi r^3&=500\\r^3&=\frac{125}{\pi}\\r&=\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}.\end{align*}$$
Also,
$$\frac{d^2S}{dr^2}=4\pi+\frac{1000}{r^3}>0\qquad\text{for all }r>0.$$
Thus the derivative is strictly increasing throughout the domain, and the stationary point gives a global minimum.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Show that to minimise the can’s surface area, the base diameter should equal its height.

answer.short: $h=\frac{10}{\pi^{1/3}}=2r$, so the height equals the base diameter.
answer.worked:
When $r=\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}$,
$$\begin{align*}h&=\frac{250}{\pi r^2}\\h&=\frac{250}{\pi\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}\right)^2}\\h&=\frac{250}{\pi\left(\frac{25}{\pi^{2/3}}\right)}\\h&=\frac{10}{\pi^{1/3}}\\h&=2r.\end{align*}$$
Hence the minimum surface area occurs when the base diameter equals the height.

content.prompt: A transport company runs a truck from Hobart to Launceston, a distance of 250 km, at a constant speed of $v$ km/h. For a given speed $v$, the cost per hour is $6400+v^2$ cents.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the cost of the trip, in cents, is $C=250\left(\frac{6400}{v}+v\right)$.

answer.worked:
The time for the trip is
$$\begin{align*}\text{time}&=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\\\text{time}&=\frac{250}{v}\text{ hours}.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}C&=(\text{cost per hour})\times(\text{time for trip})\\C&=(6400+v^2)\times\frac{250}{v}\\C&=250\left(\frac{6400}{v}+v\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the speed at which the cost of the journey is minimised.

answer.worked:
For $v>0$,
$$\begin{align*}C&=250\left(\frac{6400}{v}+v\right)\\\frac{dC}{dv}&=250\left(-\frac{6400}{v^2}+1\right)\\\frac{dC}{dv}&=\frac{250(v^2-6400)}{v^2}\\\frac{dC}{dv}&=\frac{250(v-80)(v+80)}{v^2}.\end{align*}$$
The derivative has a single zero in the domain $v>0$, at $v=80$.
$$\frac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\frac{250\times12800}{v^3}>0\qquad(v>0).$$
Therefore $v=80$ gives the global minimum in this domain. The speed is $80\text{ km/h}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the minimum cost of the journey.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}C(80)&=250\left(\frac{6400}{80}+80\right)\\C(80)&=40000\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
The minimum cost is $\$400$.

answer.short: Maximum volume: $16\,000\text{ cm}^3$. Dimensions: $40\text{ cm}\times40\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ cm be the side length of each removed square. The base is $(60-2x)$ cm by $(60-2x)$ cm and the height is $x$ cm, with $0<x<30$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Express the area of the quadrilateral $CDFE$ as a function of $x$.

answer.worked:
Subtract triangles $CBE$ and $FEA$ from the square. Since $BE=1-x$,
$$\begin{align*}A(x)&=A_{ABCD}-A_{CBE}-A_{FEA}\\A(x)&=1^2-\frac{1(1-x)}{2}-\frac{x^2}{2}\\A(x)&=\frac12+\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the greatest area that the quadrilateral can have.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A'(x)&=\frac12-x.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac12-x\\x&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
Since $A''(x)=-1<0$ throughout the domain, this gives the greatest area.
$$\begin{align*}A\left(\frac12\right)&=\frac12+\frac14-\frac18\\A\left(\frac12\right)&=\frac58.\end{align*}$$
The greatest area is $\frac58$ square units.

content.prompt: An open cylindrical water tank has base radius $x$ metres and height $h$ metres. Each square metre of the base costs $a$ dollars to manufacture and each square metre of the curved surface costs $b$ dollars. The combined cost of the base and curved surface is $c$ dollars.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find $c$ in terms of $a$, $b$, $x$ and $h$.

answer.worked:
The base area is $\pi x^2$ square metres, so its cost is $a\pi x^2$ dollars. The curved surface area is $2\pi xh$ square metres, so its cost is $2\pi bxh$ dollars.
$$c=\pi ax^2+2\pi bxh.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the tank is given by $V=\dfrac{x}{2b}(c-\pi ax^2)$.

answer.worked:
$$V=\pi x^2h.$$
From the cost equation,
$$\begin{align*}2\pi bxh&=c-\pi ax^2\\h&=\frac{c-\pi ax^2}{2\pi bx}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{align*}V&=\pi x^2\times\frac{c-\pi ax^2}{2\pi bx}\\V&=\frac{x}{2b}(c-\pi ax^2).\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: As $x$ varies, prove that $V$ is at its maximum when the cost of the base is $\dfrac{c}{3}$ dollars.

answer.short: The maximum occurs at $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{c}{3\pi a}}$, giving base cost $\pi ax^2=\dfrac{c}{3}$ dollars.
answer.worked:
For a tank with positive dimensions, $a,b,c>0$ and $0<x<\sqrt{c/(\pi a)}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dV}{dx}&=\frac{c-3\pi ax^2}{2b}.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}c-3\pi ax^2&=0\\x^2&=\frac{c}{3\pi a}\\x&=\sqrt{\frac{c}{3\pi a}}.\end{align*}$$
This value lies in the domain. Also,
$$\frac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-\frac{3\pi ax}{b}<0$$
throughout the domain, since $a,x,b>0$. Thus the stationary point gives the global maximum volume.
At this radius,
$$\begin{align*}\text{Base cost}&=a\pi x^2\\\text{Base cost}&=a\pi\times\frac{c}{3\pi a}\\\text{Base cost}&=\frac{c}{3}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore the volume is greatest when the base costs $\dfrac{c}{3}$ dollars.

content.prompt: A straight line passes through the point $(2,1)$ and has positive $x$- and $y$-intercepts at $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Suppose $\angle OPQ=\alpha$, where $O$ is the origin.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the line has gradient $-\tan\alpha$.

answer.short: The angle of inclination is $\pi-\alpha$, so $m=\tan(\pi-\alpha)=-\tan\alpha$.
answer.worked:
The angle of inclination is $\pi-\alpha$.
$$\begin{align*}m&=\tan(\pi-\alpha)\\m&=-\tan\alpha\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts in terms of $\alpha$.

answer.worked:
Using $y=mx+b$ and $m=-\tan\alpha$,
$$\begin{align*}y&=-x\tan\alpha+b\end{align*}$$
Substituting $(2,1)$,
$$\begin{align*}1&=-2\tan\alpha+b\\b&=1+2\tan\alpha\\y&=-x\tan\alpha+1+2\tan\alpha\end{align*}$$
At the $x$-intercept, $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=-x\tan\alpha+1+2\tan\alpha\\x\tan\alpha&=1+2\tan\alpha\\x&=\frac{1}{\tan\alpha}+2\end{align*}$$
Thus $P=\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan\alpha}+2,0\right)$.
At the $y$-intercept, $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=0+1+2\tan\alpha\\y&=1+2\tan\alpha\end{align*}$$
Thus $Q=(0,2\tan\alpha+1)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the area of $\triangle OPQ$ is given by $A=\dfrac{(2\tan\alpha+1)^2}{2\tan\alpha}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12bh\\A&=\frac12(2\tan\alpha+1)\left(\frac1{\tan\alpha}+2\right)\\A&=\frac12(2\tan\alpha+1)\left(\frac{1+2\tan\alpha}{\tan\alpha}\right)\\A&=\frac{(2\tan\alpha+1)^2}{2\tan\alpha}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: By letting $u=\tan\alpha$, find $\dfrac{dA}{du}$ and hence show that this area is minimised when $\tan\alpha=\dfrac12$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dA}{du}=\dfrac{(2u-1)(2u+1)}{2u^2}$. Its sign changes from negative to positive at $u=\dfrac12$, so the area is minimised when $\tan\alpha=\dfrac12$.

content.prompt: A truck travels 1500 km at an hourly cost given by $s^2+9000$ cents where $s$ is the average speed of the truck.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the cost for the trip is given by $C=1500\left(s+\frac{9000}{s}\right)$.

answer.worked:
For speed $s>0$ in km h$^{-1}$, the journey time is
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{d}{s}\\t&=\frac{1500}{s}.\end{align*}$$
The trip cost in cents is
$$\begin{align*}C&=(s^2+9000)t\\C&=(s^2+9000)\left(\frac{1500}{s}\right)\\C&=\frac{1500}{s}(s^2+9000)\\C&=1500\left(s+\frac{9000}{s}\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find, to the nearest km h$^{-1}$, the speed that minimises the cost of the trip.

answer.worked:
For $s>0$,
$$\begin{align*}C(s)&=1500s+\frac{13\,500\,000}{s}\\C'(s)&=1500-\frac{13\,500\,000}{s^2}.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}0&=1500-\frac{13\,500\,000}{s^2}\\0&=1500s^2-13\,500\,000\\s^2&=9000\\s&=30\sqrt{10}\\s&\approx94.8683.\end{align*}$$
The negative root is excluded because $s>0$.
$$C''(s)=\frac{27\,000\,000}{s^3}>0\quad(s>0).$$
Thus the stationary point is the global minimum on the positive-speed domain. The required speed is $95\text{ km h}^{-1}$ to the nearest km h$^{-1}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the cost of the trip to the nearest dollar.

answer.worked:
Use the unrounded minimising speed:
$$\begin{align*}C(30\sqrt{10})&=1500\left(30\sqrt{10}+\frac{9000}{30\sqrt{10}}\right)\\C(30\sqrt{10})&=90\,000\sqrt{10}\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
Converting to dollars,
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost}&=\frac{90\,000\sqrt{10}}{100}\\\text{Cost}&=900\sqrt{10}\text{ dollars}\\\text{Cost}&\approx\$2846.05.\end{align*}$$
The cost is $\$2846$ to the nearest dollar.

content.prompt: A 3 m piece of wire is cut into 2 pieces and bent around to form a square and a circle. Find the size of the 2 lengths, correct to 2 decimal places, that will make the total area of the square and circle a minimum.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ metres be the square's side length and $r$ metres be the circle's radius.

$$\begin{align*}P&=4x+2\pi r\\3&=4x+2\pi r\\r&=\frac{3-4x}{2\pi}\end{align*}$$

Both pieces have positive length, so $0<x<\frac34$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=x^2+\pi r^2\\A&=x^2+\pi\left(\frac{3-4x}{2\pi}\right)^2\\A&=x^2+\frac{(3-4x)^2}{4\pi}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}A'(x)&=2x+\frac{8x-6}{\pi}\\0&=2x+\frac{8x-6}{\pi}\\0&=2\pi x+8x-6\\0&=\pi x+4x-3\\3&=\pi x+4x\\x(\pi+4)&=3\\x&=\frac{3}{\pi+4}\end{align*}$$

$$A''(x)=2+\frac8\pi>0.$$

The stationary point lies in the domain and is the global minimum because $A''(x)>0$ throughout the domain.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Square perimeter}&=4\left(\frac3{\pi+4}\right)\\\text{Square perimeter}&=\frac{12}{\pi+4}\\\text{Square perimeter}&\approx1.68\text{ m}\\\text{Circle perimeter}&=3-\frac{12}{\pi+4}\\\text{Circle perimeter}&=\frac{3\pi}{\pi+4}\\\text{Circle perimeter}&\approx1.32\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the dimensions of the rectangle that will give the maximum surface area.

answer.worked:
Let the semicircular cross-section have radius $r$ metres. The width of the rectangle is $\pi r$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}30&=2x+2\pi r\\15&=x+\pi r\\x&=15-\pi r\end{align*}$$
The restrictions are $r>0$ and $x>0$, so $0<r<\frac{15}{\pi}$.
The surface area is
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi rx\\S&=\pi r(15-\pi r)\\S&=15\pi r-\pi^2r^2\\S'&=15\pi-2\pi^2r\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}0&=15\pi-2\pi^2r\\r&=\frac{15}{2\pi}.\end{align*}$$
Since $S''=-2\pi^2<0$ throughout the domain, this gives the maximum surface area.
$$\begin{align*}x&=15-\pi\left(\frac{15}{2\pi}\right)\\x&=7.5\text{ m}\\\pi r&=\pi\left(\frac{15}{2\pi}\right)\\\pi r&=7.5\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
The rectangle must be $7.5$ m by $7.5$ m.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the total length, $l$ m, of the wire fencing is given by
$$l=5x+\frac{720}{x}.$$

answer.worked:
Let $y$ m be the total horizontal length of the enclosure.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Area}&=xy\\
720&=xy\\
y&=\frac{720}{x}.
\end{align*}$$
There are five fences of length $x$ and one of length $y$.
$$\begin{align*}
l&=5x+y\\
l&=5x+\frac{720}{x},
\end{align*}$$
as required.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the minimum length of wire fencing required, showing why this is the minimum length.

answer.short: $120\,\mathrm{m}$, attained when $x=12\,\mathrm{m}$. Since $\dfrac{d^2l}{dx^2}=\dfrac{1440}{x^3}>0$ for $x>0$, this is the minimum.
answer.worked:
For $x>0$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dl}{dx}&=5-\frac{720}{x^2}\\
\frac{d^2l}{dx^2}&=\frac{1440}{x^3}.
\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point, $\dfrac{dl}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}
5-\frac{720}{x^2}&=0\\
5&=\frac{720}{x^2}\\
x^2&=144\\
x&=12 \qquad (x>0).
\end{align*}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2l}{dx^2}>0$ throughout $x>0$, the stationary point gives the global minimum.
$$\begin{align*}
l(12)&=5\times12+\frac{720}{12}\\
l(12)&=120\,\mathrm{m}.
\end{align*}$$
The minimum length of wire fencing required is $120\,\mathrm{m}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by
$$V=2\pi h(R^2-h^2).$$

answer.worked:
For a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $H$, $V=\pi r^2H$. Here,
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi x^2\times2h.\end{aligned}$$
Using Pythagoras,
$$\begin{aligned}R^2&=h^2+x^2\\x^2&=R^2-h^2.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2\pi h(R^2-h^2),\end{aligned}$$
as required.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, show that the cylinder has a maximum volume when $h=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=2\pi R^2-6\pi h^2=0$ gives $h=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}$. At this value, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\dfrac{12\pi R}{\sqrt3}<0$, so the volume is a maximum.
answer.worked:
For $0<h<R$,
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2\pi h(R^2-h^2)\\V&=2\pi R^2h-2\pi h^3\\\frac{dV}{dh}&=2\pi R^2-3\times2\pi h^2\\\frac{dV}{dh}&=2\pi R^2-6\pi h^2\\\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}&=-12\pi h.\end{aligned}$$
At a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\pi R^2-6\pi h^2&=0\\6\pi h^2&=2\pi R^2\\h^2&=\frac{R^2}{3}\\h&=\frac{R}{\sqrt3},\qquad h>0.\end{aligned}$$
When $h=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}$,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{d^2V}{dh^2}&=-12\pi\times\frac{R}{\sqrt3}<0.\end{aligned}$$
This is the only stationary point in $0<h<R$, and the volume tends to $0$ at both domain boundaries. Therefore the cylinder has its global maximum volume when $h=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}$ units.

content.prompt:
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral inscribed in a quarter of a circle centred at $A$, radius $100\text{ m}$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Solve the equation $\sin(x+15^\circ)=\cos 24^\circ$.

answer.short: $x=51^\circ+360^\circ k$ or $x=99^\circ+360^\circ k$, where $k$ is an integer.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\sin(x+15^\circ)&=\cos 24^\circ\\&=\sin(90^\circ-24^\circ)\\&=\sin 66^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$, the general solutions are:
$$\begin{align*}x+15^\circ&=66^\circ+360^\circ k &&\text{or}& x+15^\circ&=114^\circ+360^\circ k\\x&=51^\circ+360^\circ k &&\text{or}& x&=99^\circ+360^\circ k\end{align*}$$
where $k$ is an integer.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ can be expressed as $A=5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha)$.

answer.worked:
The quadrilateral can be split into $\triangle ACB$ and $\triangle ACD$.
For $\triangle ACB$:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\triangle ACB}&=\frac{1}{2}(100)(100)\sin\alpha\\&=5000\sin\alpha\end{align*}$$
For $\triangle ACD$, the included angle is $90^\circ-\alpha$:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\triangle ACD}&=\frac{1}{2}(100)(100)\sin(90^\circ-\alpha)\\&=5000\cos\alpha\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}A&=A_{\triangle ACB}+A_{\triangle ACD}\\&=5000\sin\alpha+5000\cos\alpha\\&=5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha)\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Using calculus, show that the maximum area of this quadrilateral is $5000\sqrt{2}\text{ m}^2$.

answer.short: Stationary point at $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is a maximum, with $A_{\max}=5000\sqrt{2}\text{ m}^2$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A&=5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha)\\\frac{dA}{d\alpha}&=5000(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha)\end{align*}$$
For a stationary point:
$$\begin{align*}5000(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha)&=0\\\cos\alpha&=\sin\alpha\\\tan\alpha&=1\\\alpha&=\frac{\pi}{4}\end{align*}$$
Check the second derivative:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}&=5000(-\sin\alpha-\cos\alpha)\end{align*}$$
At $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}&=5000\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\\&=-5000\sqrt{2}\\&<0\end{align*}$$
Therefore the stationary point gives a maximum.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\max}&=5000\left(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}+\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\&=5000\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\\&=5000\sqrt{2}\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

children.prompt:
Show that the combined area of the circle and equilateral triangle is given by
$$A(x) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}x^2 + \frac{(100 - 3x)^2}{\pi}\right)$$

answer.worked:
The circumference and the triangle's perimeter total $100\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}
2\pi r + 3x &= 100 \\
r &= \frac{100 - 3x}{2\pi}
\end{align*}$$
Area of the triangle: $\frac{1}{2} x^2 \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^2$.
$$\begin{align*}
A(x) &= \pi \left(\frac{100 - 3x}{2\pi}\right)^2 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^2 \\
&= \frac{(100 - 3x)^2}{4\pi} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}x^2 + \frac{(100 - 3x)^2}{\pi}\right)
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: By considering the quadratic function in part (a), show that the maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all the wire is used for the circle.

answer.short: $A(x)$ is a concave up quadratic, so its maximum is at an endpoint of $0\leq x\leq\frac{100}{3}$. $A(0)\approx 795.8>A\left(\frac{100}{3}\right)\approx 481.1$.
answer.worked:
The coefficient of $x^2$ is positive ($\sqrt{3}+\frac{9}{\pi}$ before the factor $\frac14$), so $A(x)$ is concave up.
The maximum on $0\leq x\leq\frac{100}{3}$ is at an endpoint.
$$\begin{align*}
A(0) &= \frac{2500}{\pi} \approx 795.8 \text{ cm}^2 \\
A\left(\frac{100}{3}\right) &= \frac{2500\sqrt{3}}{9} \approx 481.1 \text{ cm}^2
\end{align*}$$
Since $A(0) > A\left(\frac{100}{3}\right)$, the maximum occurs at $x = 0$, so all the wire is used for the circle.

Two dangerous goods long-haul drivers are contracted to share the driving on one truckload of chemicals over a distance of $1200$ km.
They are each paid \$55 per hour for the time spent on the road.
The truck consumes fuel at a rate of $10+\frac{v^2}{100}$ litres per hour where the average speed of the truck is $v$ km per hour.

$C=\frac{150\,000}{v}+18v$,

answer.worked:
Time: $T=\dfrac{1200}{v}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Wages}&=110\times\frac{1200}{v}=\frac{132\,000}{v}\\\text{Fuel cost}&=1.50\left(10+\frac{v^2}{100}\right)\frac{1200}{v}=\frac{18\,000}{v}+18v\\C&=\frac{150\,000}{v}+18v\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dC}{dv}&=-\frac{150\,000}{v^2}+18\\0&=-\frac{150\,000}{v^2}+18\\v^2&=\frac{25\,000}{3}\\v&\approx91.287\end{align*}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\dfrac{300\,000}{v^3}>0$ for $v>0$, this is a minimum.
$$C\approx1643.17+1643.17\approx3286$$
The minimum cost is approximately \$3286.

children.prompt: The garden bed is required to have an area of $36\text{ m}^2$ and to have a perimeter which is as small as possible. Let $P$ metres be the perimeter of the garden bed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $P=2x+\dfrac{72}{x}$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=xy+\frac14\pi r^2\\36&=xy+\frac14\pi x^2\\xy&=36-\frac{\pi x^2}{4}\\y&=\frac{36}{x}-\frac{\pi x}{4}\end{align*}$$
The perimeter includes the two horizontal rectangle edges, the left edge, the exposed horizontal radius and the quarter-circle arc.
$$\begin{align*}P&=2x+2y+\frac14(2\pi x)\\P&=2x+2\left(\frac{36}{x}-\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)+\frac{\pi x}{2}\\P&=2x+\frac{72}{x}-\frac{\pi x}{2}+\frac{\pi x}{2}\\P&=2x+\frac{72}{x}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the smallest possible perimeter of the garden bed, showing why this is the minimum perimeter.

answer.short: The smallest possible perimeter is $24\text{ m}$, attained at $x=6\text{ m}$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P&=2x+\frac{72}{x}\\\frac{dP}{dx}&=2-72x^{-2}\\\frac{d^2P}{dx^2}&=144x^{-3}\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point, $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}2-\frac{72}{x^2}&=0\\2x^2&=72\\x^2&=36\\x&=6\qquad(x>0)\end{align*}$$
When $x=6$,
$$\frac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\frac{144}{6^3}=\frac23>0.$$
Thus $\Rightarrow$ a minimum at $x=6$. Also, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2}>0$ throughout the feasible domain, so this is the global minimum. The value is feasible because $y=6-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}>0$.
$$\begin{align*}P_{\min}&=2\times6+\frac{72}{6}\\P_{\min}&=24\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: A particle is shot vertically upwards from a point 100 metres above ground level.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the maximum height above ground level reached by the particle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y(t)&=-5t^2+70t+100\\y'(t)&=-10t+70\\y''(t)&=-10\end{aligned}$$
The maximum occurs when $y'(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-10t+70&=0\\10t&=70\\t&=7\end{aligned}$$
Since $y''(t)=-10<0$ throughout the flight, this is the maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}y(7)&=-5(7)^2+70\times7+100\\y(7)&=345\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the velocity of the particle, in metres per second, immediately before it hits the ground, leaving your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

answer.worked:
The particle hits the ground when $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-5t^2+70t+100\\0&=t^2-14t-20\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{14\pm\sqrt{14^2+4\times20}}{2}\\t&=\frac{14+\sqrt{276}}{2}\qquad(t>0)\\t&=7+\sqrt{69}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}v(t)&=y'(t)\\v(t)&=-10t+70\\v(7+\sqrt{69})&=-10(7+\sqrt{69})+70\\v(7+\sqrt{69})&=-10\sqrt{69}\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
Thus $a=-10$ and $b=69$.

content.prompt:
An open-topped fish tank of volume $90\text{ m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism of length $2x$ metres, width $x$ metres, and height $h$ metres.
Materials cost \$15 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$20 per square metre for the sides of the tank.
Show that the total cost $C$ of making the fish tank is given by
$$C = 30x^2 + \frac{5400}{x}$$
and hence find the dimensions of the fish tank with the least total cost.

answer.short: Length $2\sqrt[3]{90}$ m, width $\sqrt[3]{90}$ m, height $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{90}}{2}$ m.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2x^2h&=90\\h&=\frac{45}{x^2}\end{align*}$$
Base cost: $15(2x^2)=30x^2$. Side area: $2(2xh)+2(xh)=6xh$, so side cost: $120xh=120x\left(\frac{45}{x^2}\right)=\frac{5400}{x}$.
$$C=30x^2+\frac{5400}{x}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dC}{dx}&=60x-\frac{5400}{x^2}\\0&=60x-\frac{5400}{x^2}\\x^3&=90\\x&=\sqrt[3]{90}\end{align*}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=60+\dfrac{10800}{x^3}>0$ for $x>0$, this is a minimum.
Height: $h=\dfrac{45}{x^2}=\dfrac{x^3/2}{x^2}=\dfrac{x}{2}$.
The dimensions are length $2\sqrt[3]{90}$ m, width $\sqrt[3]{90}$ m and height $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{90}}{2}$ m.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine a volume constraint with different base and side costs, minimise the supplied cost function and interpret the result as three dimensions.

content.prompt:
A closed cylindrical tank has a circular base of radius $r$ metres and a height of $h$ metres.
It can hold $160\pi\text{ m}^3$ of wheat.
The material for the flat circular top and bottom costs \$10 per square metre and the material for the curved surface costs \$8 per square metre.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the height of the tank is $h=\frac{160}{r^2}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\pi r^2h&=160\pi\\h&=\frac{160}{r^2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the dimensions of the tank that minimise the cost of construction.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}C&=10(2\pi r^2)+8(2\pi rh)\\&=20\pi r^2+16\pi r\left(\frac{160}{r^2}\right)\\&=20\pi r^2+\frac{2560\pi}{r}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}C'&=40\pi r-\frac{2560\pi}{r^2}\\0&=40\pi r-\frac{2560\pi}{r^2}\\r^3&=64\\r&=4\end{align*}$$
Since $C''=40\pi+\dfrac{5120\pi}{r^3}>0$ for $r>0$, this is a minimum.
$$h=\frac{160}{4^2}=10$$
The radius is $4$ m and the height is $10$ m.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the volume constraint to construct a cost function from differently priced cylindrical surfaces, then minimise it and recover both dimensions.

content.prompt:
John's home is at point $A$ and his school is at point $B$.
A straight river runs nearby.
The point on the river closest to $A$ is point $C$, which is $5 \text{ km}$ from $A$.
The point on the river closest to $B$ is point $D$, which is $7 \text{ km}$ from $B$.
The distance from $C$ to $D$ is $9 \text{ km}$.
To get some exercise, John cycles from home directly to point $E$ on the river, $x \text{ km}$ from $C$, before cycling directly to school at $B$, as shown in the diagram.
The total distance John cycles from home to school is $L \text{ km}$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that $L=\sqrt{x^2+25}+\sqrt{49+(9-x)^2}$.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ACE$:
$AE=\sqrt{5^2+x^2}=\sqrt{x^2+25}$.
In $\triangle BDE$, $ED=9-x$:
$BE=\sqrt{7^2+(9-x)^2}=\sqrt{49+(9-x)^2}$.
$$\begin{align*}L&=AE+BE\\&=\sqrt{x^2+25}+\sqrt{49+(9-x)^2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that if $\frac{dL}{dx}=0$, then $\sin \alpha=\sin \beta$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dL}{dx} &= \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 25}} - \frac{9 - x}{\sqrt{49 + (9 - x)^2}}
\end{align*}$$
If $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:
$$\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 25}} = \frac{9 - x}{\sqrt{49 + (9 - x)^2}}$$
In $\triangle ACE$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+25}}$.
In $\triangle BDE$, $\sin\beta=\dfrac{9-x}{\sqrt{(9-x)^2+49}}$.
Therefore $\sin\alpha=\sin\beta$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Find the value of $x$ that makes $\sin \alpha=\sin \beta$.

answer.worked:
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are acute, so $\alpha=\beta$ and $\triangle ACE$ is similar to $\triangle BDE$.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{x}{5} &= \frac{9 - x}{7} \\
7x &= 45 - 5x \\
12x &= 45 \\
x &= 3\frac{3}{4}
\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Explain why this value of $x$ gives a minimum for $L$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dL}{dx}<0$ at $x=0$ and $\dfrac{dL}{dx}>0$ at $x=9$, and there is only one stationary point, so it is a minimum.
answer.worked:
At $x=0$: $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=-\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{130}}<0$.
At $x=9$: $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{106}}>0$.
The derivative changes from negative to positive and there is only one stationary point, $x=3\frac{3}{4}$, in $0<x<9$.
So it is a minimum.

content.prompt:
An oil rig, $S$, is $3 \text{ km}$ offshore.
A power station, $P$, is on the shore.
A cable is to be laid from $P$ to $S$.
It costs $\$1000$ per kilometre to lay the cable along the shore and $\$2600$ per kilometre to lay the cable underwater from the shore to $S$.
The point $R$ is the point on the shore closest to $S$, and the distance $PR$ is $5 \text{ km}$.
The point $Q$ is on the shore, at a distance of $x \text{ km}$ from $R$, as shown in the diagram.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the total cost of laying the cable in a straight line from $P$ to $R$ and then in a straight line from $R$ to $S$.

answer.worked:
$PR$ is $5 \text{ km}$ along the shore and $RS$ is $3 \text{ km}$ underwater.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Total cost} &= 5 \times 1000 + 3 \times 2600 \\
&= 5000 + 7800 \\
&= \$12800
\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the cost of laying the cable in a straight line from $P$ to $S$.

answer.worked:
$PS=\sqrt{5^2+3^2}=\sqrt{34}\text{ km}$, all underwater.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Cost} &= 2600 \times \sqrt{34} \\
&\approx \$15160.47
\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Let $\$C$ be the total cost of laying the cable in a straight line from $P$ to $Q$, and then in a straight line from $Q$ to $S$.
Show that $C = 1000(5 - x + 2.6\sqrt{x^2 + 9})$.

answer.worked:
$PQ = 5 - x \text{ km}$ along the shore and $QS = \sqrt{x^2 + 9} \text{ km}$ underwater.
$$\begin{align*}
C &= 1000(5 - x) + 2600\sqrt{x^2 + 9} \\
&= 1000(5 - x + 2.6\sqrt{x^2 + 9})
\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Find the minimum cost of laying the cable.

answer.short:
$\$12200$, when $x=1.25\text{ km}$.
Method: solve $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$, then check the endpoint costs are larger.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dC}{dx} &= 1000\left(-1 + \frac{2.6x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9}}\right)
\end{align*}$$
Let $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}
2.6x &= \sqrt{x^2 + 9} \\
6.76x^2 &= x^2 + 9 \\
5.76x^2 &= 9 \\
x &= 1.25
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
C(1.25) &= 1000(3.75 + 2.6\times 3.25) \\
&= \$12200
\end{align*}$$
The endpoint costs are $C(0)=\$12800$ and $C(5)\approx\$15160$, both larger.
The minimum cost is $\$12200$.

children.label: v
children.prompt:
New technology means that the cost of laying the cable underwater can be reduced to $\$1100$ per kilometre.
Determine the path for laying the cable in order to minimise the cost in this case.

answer.short: Lay the cable in a straight line from $P$ to $S$ ($x=5$).
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
C &= 1000(5 - x + 1.1\sqrt{x^2 + 9}) \\
\frac{dC}{dx} &= 1000\left(-1 + \frac{1.1x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9}}\right)
\end{align*}$$
Let $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}
1.21x^2 &= x^2 + 9 \\
x^2 &= \frac{9}{0.21} \\
x &\approx 6.55
\end{align*}$$
This is outside the domain $0 \leq x \leq 5$.
On $[0,5]$, $\dfrac{dC}{dx}<0$, so $C$ is decreasing and the minimum is at $x=5$.
The cable should be laid in a straight line from $P$ to $S$.

content.prompt:
A sector with radius $10\text{ cm}$ and angle $\theta$ is used to form the curved surface of a cone with base radius $x\text{ cm}$, as shown in the diagram.

The volume of a cone of radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by $V=\frac13\pi r^2h$.

spec.description: Major sector at left and the cone formed from it at right. The reflex angle arrow follows the retained major sector. The cone has a solid front base boundary, dashed rear boundary, dashed internal height and radius, and a right-angle marker. Both figures remain together in one editable vector.
spec.mathematics: Sector radius and cone slant height are 10 cm. The retained sector angle is theta, not the removed wedge angle. Cone base radius is x cm; height is perpendicular to the base radius.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and construction lines are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the volume, $V\text{ cm}^3$, of the cone described above is given by
$$V=\left(\frac13\right)\pi x^2\sqrt{100-x^2}.$$

answer.worked:
Using Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}h^2+x^2&=10^2\\h&=\sqrt{100-x^2}.\end{align*}$$
Since $r=x$,
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac13\pi r^2h\\V&=\frac13\pi x^2\sqrt{100-x^2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $\displaystyle\frac{dV}{dx}=\frac{\pi x(200-3x^2)}{3\sqrt{100-x^2}}$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac13\pi x^2\sqrt{100-x^2}\\\frac{dV}{dx}&=\frac13\pi\left[2x\sqrt{100-x^2}-2x\cdot\frac12(100-x^2)^{-1/2}\cdot x^2\right]\\\frac{dV}{dx}&=\frac13\pi\left[\frac{2x(100-x^2)-x^3}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}\right]\\\frac{dV}{dx}&=\frac13\pi\left[\frac{200x-2x^3-x^3}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}\right]\\\frac{dV}{dx}&=\frac{\pi x(200-3x^2)}{3\sqrt{100-x^2}}.\end{align*}$$
As required.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the exact value of $\theta$ for which $V$ is a maximum.

answer.worked:
For a non-degenerate cone, $0<x<10$. Find $x$ when $\frac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}200-3x^2&=0\\x&=\sqrt{\frac{200}{3}}.\end{align*}$$
When $0<x<\sqrt{\frac{200}{3}}$, $200-3x^2>0$:
$$\Rightarrow\quad\frac{dV}{dx}>0.$$
When $\sqrt{\frac{200}{3}}<x<10$, $200-3x^2<0$:
$$\Rightarrow\quad\frac{dV}{dx}<0.$$
Thus $V$ increases and then decreases throughout the domain, so its global maximum occurs at $x=\sqrt{\frac{200}{3}}$.

Equate the sector arc length to the circumference of the cone's base. With $\theta$ in radians,
$$\begin{align*}2\pi(10)\cdot\frac{\theta}{2\pi}&=2\pi x\\10\theta&=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{200}{3}}\\\theta&=\frac{2\pi\cdot10\sqrt2}{10\sqrt3}\\\theta&=\frac{2\sqrt2\pi}{\sqrt3}\text{ radians}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The figure shown represents a wire frame where $ABCE$ is a convex quadrilateral.

The point $D$ is on line segment $EC$ with $AB=ED=2$ cm and $BC=a$ cm, where $a$ is a positive constant.

Let $\angle CBD=\theta$, where $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$.

spec.description: Rectangle ABDE beneath right triangle BDC, including internal wire BD, three right-angle marks and angle CBD.
spec.mathematics: AB=ED=2 cm; BC=a cm; D lies on EC; angle CBD=theta.
spec.answerVisibility: question

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find $BD$ and $CD$ in terms of $a$ and $\theta$.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle BCD$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{BD}{a}\\BD&=a\cos\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{CD}{a}\\CD&=a\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the length, $L$ cm, of the wire in the frame, including length $BD$, in terms of $a$ and $\theta$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}L&=4+2BD+CD+a\\L&=4+2a\cos\theta+a\sin\theta+a\\L&=4+a+2a\cos\theta+a\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find $\frac{dL}{d\theta}$, and hence show that $\frac{dL}{d\theta}=0$ when $BD=2CD$.

answer.worked:
Noting that $a$ is a constant:
$$\frac{dL}{d\theta}=-2a\sin\theta+a\cos\theta.$$
When $\frac{dL}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}-2a\sin\theta+a\cos\theta&=0\\a\cos\theta&=2a\sin\theta\\BD&=2CD\end{align*}$$
The last line uses part (a).

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the maximum value of $L$ if $a=3\sqrt5$.

answer.worked:
Stationary points occur when $\frac{dL}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{align*}-2a\sin\theta+a\cos\theta&=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\cos\theta\\\tan\theta&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
The reference triangle gives $\cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$ and $\sin\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$.

$$\frac{d^2L}{d\theta^2}=-2a\cos\theta-a\sin\theta<0\qquad\left(0<\theta<\frac\pi2\right).$$
Thus $L'$ is strictly decreasing throughout the domain, and its unique zero gives the global maximum.
$$\begin{align*}L_{\max}&=4+a+2a\cos\theta+a\sin\theta\\L_{\max}&=4+3\sqrt5+2(3\sqrt5)\left(\frac2{\sqrt5}\right)+(3\sqrt5)\left(\frac1{\sqrt5}\right)\\L_{\max}&=4+3\sqrt5+12+3\\L_{\max}&=19+3\sqrt5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Two circles have the same centre $O$.

The smaller circle has radius $1$ cm, while the larger circle has radius $(1+x)$ cm.

The circles enclose a region $QRST$, which is subtended by an angle $\theta$ at $O$, as shaded.

The area of $QRST$ is $A$ cm², where $A$ is a constant and $A>0$.

Let $P$ cm be the perimeter of $QRST$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 12, diagram to the right of the stem
spec.description: Complete concentric circles with an upward annular sector QRST. Q and T lie on the left radius; R and S lie on the right radius. The shaded region is retained using a light house-blue fill. Schematic radii do not assign a numerical value to x.
spec.mathematics: OT=OS=1 cm; TQ=SR=x cm; OQ=OR=1+x cm; angle QOR=theta. The assessed region is bounded by arcs QR and TS and segments QT and RS.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens and shaded region appear.

children.label: a
children.prompt: By finding expressions for the area and perimeter of $QRST$, show that $P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$.

answer.worked:
Area = sector $OQR$ − sector $OTS$.
$$\begin{align*}
A&=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times\pi(1+x)^2-\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times\pi\times1^2\\
A&=\frac{\theta}{2}(1+x)^2-\frac{\theta}{2}\\
A&=\frac{\theta}{2}(1+2x+x^2-1)\\
A&=\frac{\theta}{2}x(x+2)\\
\theta&=\frac{2A}{x(x+2)}.
\end{align*}$$
The perimeter includes both arcs and the two radial sides:
$$\begin{align*}
P&=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times2\pi(x+1)+\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times2\pi(1)+2x\\
P&=\theta(x+1)+\theta+2x\\
P&=\theta(x+2)+2x\\
P&=\frac{2A}{x(x+2)}(x+2)+2x\\
P(x)&=2x+\frac{2A}{x}.
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that if the perimeter, $P(x)$, is minimised, then $\theta$ must be less than $2$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
P(x)&=2x+\frac{2A}{x}\\
P'(x)&=2-\frac{2A}{x^2}\\
P''(x)&=\frac{4A}{x^3}>0\qquad(x,A>0).
\end{align*}$$
Thus $P'$ is increasing, and the stationary point gives the minimum. Set $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{align*}
2-\frac{2A}{x^2}&=0\\
2x^2&=2A\\
x^2&=A.
\end{align*}$$
Using part (a):
$$\begin{align*}
\theta&=\frac{2A}{x(x+2)}\\
\theta&=\frac{2x^2}{x(x+2)}\\
\theta&=\frac{2x}{x+2}\\
\theta&=2\times\frac{x}{x+2}\\
\theta&<2.
\end{align*}$$
Since $x>0$, $0<\frac{x}{x+2}<1$. Therefore, if $P(x)$ is minimised, $\theta<2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $xy=24$.

answer.worked:
Triangles $TPQ$ and $TSU$ are similar, so
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{x+4}&=\frac{6}{y+6}\\x(y+6)&=6(x+4)\\xy+6x&=6x+24\\xy&=24.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the area of $\triangle TSU$ is given by $A=24+3x+\dfrac{48}{x}$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{bh}{2}\\A&=\frac{(x+4)(y+6)}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Since $xy=24$, $y=\dfrac{24}{x}$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{(x+4)\left(\frac{24}{x}+6\right)}{2}\\A&=\frac{24+6x+\frac{96}{x}+24}{2}\\A&=24+3x+\frac{48}{x}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence find the minimum possible area of $\triangle TSU$.

answer.short: The minimum possible area is $48\text{ cm}^2$, attained when $x=4\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
The domain is $x>0$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dA}{dx}&=3-\frac{48}{x^2}.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}3-\frac{48}{x^2}&=0\\3x^2-48&=0\\3(x^2-16)&=0\\x&=4\qquad(x>0).\end{align*}$$
Checking the minimum:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2A}{dx^2}&=\frac{96}{x^3}\\A''(4)&=\frac{96}{64}>0.\end{align*}$$
Since $A''(x)>0$ throughout $x>0$, this stationary point is the global minimum.
$$\begin{align*}A(4)&=24+3(4)+\frac{48}{4}\\A(4)&=48.\end{align*}$$
The minimum possible area is $48\text{ cm}^2$.

content.prompt:
A closed rectangular box has length $x$ cm, width $y$ cm and height $h$ cm.

It is to be made from $300\text{ cm}^2$ of thin sheet metal, and the perimeter of the base is to be $40$ cm.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the box is given by $V=150h-20h^2$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}V&=xyh\\P&=2x+2y=40\\x+y&=20\end{align*}$$

The box is closed, so its surface area is
$$\begin{align*}A&=2xy+2xh+2yh\\300&=2xy+2xh+2yh\\150&=xy+xh+yh\\150&=xy+h(x+y)\\150&=xy+20h\\xy&=150-20h.\end{align*}$$

Substitute into $V=xyh$:
$$\begin{align*}V&=(150-20h)h\\V&=150h-20h^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence find the dimensions of the box that meets all the requirements and has the maximum possible volume.

answer.short: $15\text{ cm}\times5\text{ cm}\times3.75\text{ cm}$, with height $3.75$ cm.
answer.worked:
Since $x,y>0$ and $x+y=20$, the base area satisfies $0<xy\le100$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}0&<150-20h\le100\\2.5&\le h<7.5.\end{align*}$$

Find the stationary point:
$$\begin{align*}V(h)&=150h-20h^2\\V'(h)&=150-40h\\150-40h&=0\\h&=3.75\\V''(h)&=-40<0.\end{align*}$$

The volume function is concave down throughout the feasible domain, so its global maximum occurs at $h=3.75$ cm.

Recover the base dimensions:
$$\begin{align*}150&=xy+20(3.75)\\150&=xy+75\\xy&=75\\x+y&=20\\y&=20-x.\end{align*}$$

Substitute into $xy=75$:
$$\begin{align*}x(20-x)&=75\\x^2-20x+75&=0\\(x-5)(x-15)&=0\\x&=5\text{ or }15.\end{align*}$$

The corresponding values of $y$ are $15$ or $5$. Therefore the dimensions are $15$ cm by $5$ cm by $3.75$ cm.

Check: the base perimeter is $2(15+5)=40$ cm, and the surface area is $2(15)(5)+2(15)(3.75)+2(5)(3.75)=300\text{ cm}^2$.

content.prompt: A symmetrical gutter is made from a sheet of metal 30 cm wide by bending it twice as shown:

spec.sourceRegion: Question 30, below the parts on the left
spec.description: Open symmetrical trapezoidal gutter with equal-length ticks on the bottom and both sloping sides. Dotted verticals rise from the bottom corners to the dotted horizontal joining the upper endpoints. Each theta lies between a side and its adjacent vertical. The diagram is unshaded, with ordinary marks in black.
spec.mathematics: The bottom is 10 cm. Matching ticks and the 30 cm total sheet width establish that both sloping sides are also 10 cm. Theta is measured from the vertical.
spec.answerVisibility: All measurements, equal-length marks, guides and angle labels are permanent givens; no calculated dimensions or optimum angle are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the cross-sectional area of the gutter is given by $A=100\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)\,\mathrm{cm}^2$.

answer.worked:
The total sheet width is 30 cm and the base is 10 cm. Each equal sloping side therefore has length 10 cm. Since $\theta$ is measured from the vertical, the vertical height is $10\cos\theta$ cm and the horizontal projection of each side is $10\sin\theta$ cm.

The cross-section is a trapezium with lower base 10 cm, upper base $10+2(10\sin\theta)=10+20\sin\theta$ cm and height $10\cos\theta$ cm. Using $A=\frac12(a+b)h$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac12(10+10+20\sin\theta)(10\cos\theta)\\A&=\frac12(20+20\sin\theta)(10\cos\theta)\\A&=100\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: For what value of $\theta$ does the gutter have maximum carrying capacity?

answer.worked:
Use radians, with $0\leq\theta\leq\frac\pi2$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=100\cos\theta+100\cos\theta\sin\theta\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=-100\sin\theta+100(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta).\end{aligned}$$
Using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=100(-\sin\theta+1-2\sin^2\theta)\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=-100(2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1).\end{aligned}$$
For $\frac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta=-1.\end{aligned}$$
There is no solution to $\sin\theta=-1$ in the domain. Thus
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=\frac\pi6.\end{aligned}$$
Check the maximum:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-100(4\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos\theta)\\A''\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=-150\sqrt3<0.\end{aligned}$$
This is the only interior stationary point. Also, $A(0)=100$ and $A(\frac\pi2)=0$, whereas $A(\frac\pi6)=75\sqrt3>100$. The maximum carrying capacity occurs at $\theta=\frac\pi6$ radians $(30^\circ)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the cross-sectional area for this value of $\theta$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=100\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\left(1+\frac12\right)\\A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=100\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\left(\frac32\right)\\A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=75\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\end{aligned}$$
The cross-sectional area is $75\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm}^2$, approximately $130\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ to the nearest square centimetre.

inlines.text: Sophie needs to get from point A to point B across a wide river.
The river is 20 m wide, and B is 80 m horizontally from A.
She swims across the river at a speed of 7 km/h and runs at 11 km/h.
that will minimise her total travel time. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

spec.description: Parallel banks, A on the upper bank, B farther right on the lower bank and a diagonal swimming segment x to a landing point before B. The vertical dimension is 20 m; the complete horizontal displacement from A to B is 80 m. Source blue lines are ordinary geometry and use house black.
spec.mathematics: Swimming distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle of height 20 m; running distance is 80 m minus its horizontal leg.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no landing distance or solution supplied.

answer.worked:
Let $y$ m be the horizontal distance from directly opposite A to the landing point. Then $x^2=20^2+y^2$, so $y=\sqrt{x^2-400}$ and the running distance is $80-\sqrt{x^2-400}$ m. Using speeds $7000$ m/h and $11\,000$ m/h,
$$\begin{aligned}T(x)&=\frac{x}{7000}+\frac{80-\sqrt{x^2-400}}{11\,000},\qquad 20\le x\le20\sqrt{17}\\T'(x)&=\frac{1}{7000}-\frac{x}{11\,000\sqrt{x^2-400}}.\end{aligned}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7000}&=\frac{x}{11\,000\sqrt{x^2-400}}\\11\sqrt{x^2-400}&=7x\\121(x^2-400)&=49x^2\\72x^2&=48\,400\\x^2&=\frac{6050}{9}\\x&=\frac{55\sqrt2}{3}.\end{aligned}$$
For $x>20$,
$$T''(x)=\frac{400}{11\,000(x^2-400)^{3/2}}>0.$$
Thus $T'$ is increasing and changes from negative to positive at this stationary point, giving the global minimum on the domain. Sophie should swim $\frac{55\sqrt2}{3}\text{ m}\approx25.9\text{ m}$.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the geometric constraint for a cone inscribed in a sphere, optimise a symbolic volume function and interpret the resulting ratio.

content.prompt:
A cone of height $h$ is inscribed in a sphere of constant radius $R$.
Find the ratio $h:R$ when the volume of the cone is maximised.

answer.worked:
Let $r$ be the cone's base radius. The distance from the sphere's centre to the base plane is $|h-R|$, so
$$\begin{align*}r^2+(h-R)^2&=R^2\\r^2&=2Rh-h^2.\end{align*}$$
For $0<h<2R$,
$$\begin{align*}V(h)&=\frac{\pi r^2h}{3}\\V(h)&=\frac{\pi}{3}(2Rh^2-h^3)\\V'(h)&=\frac{\pi}{3}(4Rh-3h^2).\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}h(4R-3h)&=0\\h&=\frac{4R}{3}\qquad(h>0).\end{align*}$$
Check the maximum:
$$\begin{align*}V''(h)&=\frac{\pi}{3}(4R-6h)\\V''\left(\frac{4R}{3}\right)&=-\frac{4\pi R}{3}<0.\end{align*}$$
This is the only stationary point in the domain, and the volume tends to zero at both ends. Hence it gives the global maximum.
$$h:R=\frac{4R}{3}:R=4:3.$$

content.prompt: An isosceles triangle $PQR$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ of radius 1 unit, as shown in the diagram. Let $\angle QOR=2\theta$, where $\theta$ is acute.

spec.description: Unshaded circle with an inscribed isosceles triangle, matching single ticks on PQ and PR, dashed radii OQ and OR, and the central angle labelled 2θ. The construction through P and O and point M are absent.
spec.mathematics: OP=OQ=OR=1; PQ=PR; P lies on the perpendicular bisector of chord QR; angle QOR=2θ. Coordinates provide a schematic view and supply no numerical angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; M and the requested construction are reserved for the response.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Join $PO$ and extend it to meet $QR$ at $M$. Then prove that $QM=\sin\theta$ and $OM=\cos\theta$.

answer.short: $QM=\sin\theta$ and $OM=\cos\theta$, using right triangle $OQM$ with hypotenuse $OQ=1$.
answer.worked:
Since $PQ=PR$ and $OQ=OR$, both $P$ and $O$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $QR$. Thus the line $PO$ meets $QR$ at its midpoint $M$ and $OM\perp QR$. The congruent right triangles $OQM$ and $ORM$ give $\angle QOM=\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{QM}{OQ}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{QM}{1}\\\sin\theta&=QM,\\\cos\theta&=\frac{OM}{OQ}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{OM}{1}\\\cos\theta&=OM.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Complete solution figure adds PM through O, the midpoint M, a derived right-angle mark and the two equal central half-angles.
spec.mathematics: M is the midpoint of QR, PM is perpendicular to QR, and angle QOM=angle MOR=θ.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution-only construction and derived angle labels.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the area $A$ of $\triangle PQR$ is $A=\sin\theta(\cos\theta+1)$.

answer.worked:
$QR=2QM$ and $PM=PO+OM$, with $PO=1$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12 bh\\A&=\frac12 QR\times PM\\A&=\frac12(2QM)(PO+OM)\\A&=\frac12\cdot2\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\\A&=\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta).\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence show that, as $\theta$ varies, $\triangle PQR$ has its maximum possible area when it is equilateral.

answer.short: The maximum occurs at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Then $\angle QOR=\angle POQ=\angle POR=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, so the equal chords $PQ$, $PR$ and $QR$ form an equilateral triangle.
answer.worked:
For $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$,

$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\\A&=\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta\\A&=\sin\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta,\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=\cos\theta+2\cos^2\theta-1\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1).\end{align*}$$

At a stationary point,

$$\begin{align*}(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$

Thus $2\cos\theta-1=0$ or $\cos\theta+1=0$. Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta>0$, so $\cos\theta=-1$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos\theta&=1\\\cos\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$

Check the maximum:

$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-\sin\theta-2\sin2\theta\\\left.\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}\right|_{\theta=\pi/3}&=-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}<0.\end{align*}$$

This stationary point is a maximum. Moreover, $\cos\theta+1>0$, so $\frac{dA}{d\theta}>0$ before $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{dA}{d\theta}<0$ after it throughout the acute domain. Hence it is the global maximum.

Triangles $POQ$ and $POR$ are congruent by SSS: $PO$ is common, $OQ=OR$ and $PQ=PR$. Therefore $\angle POQ=\angle POR$. At the maximum,

$$\begin{align*}\angle QOR&=2\theta\\\angle QOR&=\frac{2\pi}{3},\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac12(2\pi-\angle QOR)\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac12\left(2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac{2\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$

The vertices are evenly spaced around the circle. Equal central angles subtend equal chords, so $PQ=PR=QR$ and the triangle is equilateral.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] The only worked example is a cubic on a closed interval, but five later questions use a reciprocal term on an open domain x>0 and need a global-extremum justification without endpoints. Add a worked example of this type after the box-net example.
Worked example: A rectangular paddock of area $450\text{ m}^2$ is to be fenced on three sides, with the fourth side along a straight wall.

Find the dimensions of the paddock that minimise the length of fencing, and the minimum length.
1.
Let the paddock be $x$ m wide (perpendicular to the wall) and $y$ m long (along the wall).
$$\begin{aligned}xy&=450\\y&=\frac{450}{x}\end{aligned}$$
The fence runs along two widths and one length.
$$\begin{aligned}L&=2x+y\\L(x)&=2x+\frac{450}{x}\end{aligned}$$

2.
$x$ must be positive, and every positive $x$ gives a paddock, so there is no upper limit.
$x>0$

3.
Find stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned}L'(x)&=2-\frac{450}{x^2}=0\\2&=\frac{450}{x^2}\\\color{#ef6068}{x^2\times}\,2&=\color{#ef6068}{x^2\times}\,\frac{450}{x^2}\\2x^2&=450\\x^2&=225\\x&=15\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Checking minimum:
$$L''(x)=\frac{900}{x^3}>0\quad\text{for all }x>0$$
The graph is concave up on the whole domain, so the only stationary point is the global minimum. The domain has no endpoints, and $L$ becomes very large as $x\to0^+$ and as $x\to\infty$.

4.
$y=\dfrac{450}{15}=30$.
The paddock should be 15 m wide and 30 m long. The minimum length of fencing is $L(15)=2(15)+30=60\text{ m}$.
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Solve each problem.
a) A rectangular field of area $150\text{ m}^2$ is fenced all round and divided into two equal paddocks by a fence parallel to one pair of its sides, as shown.

Find the dimensions of the field that minimise the length of fencing, and the minimum length. (with a diagram)
b) An open box with a square base is to have a volume of $32\text{ cm}^3$.

Find the base side length that minimises the surface area of the box, and the minimum surface area.
Answers: a) $x=10\text{ m}$ and $y=15\text{ m}$. The minimum length of fencing is $60\text{ m}$.; b) Base side length $4\text{ cm}$. The minimum surface area is $48\text{ cm}^2$.
Comparison score: 52.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] The booklet never shows how to solve dT/dx=0 when the time function contains a square root: isolate the radical, square both sides, then check the root is in the domain. The rowing question needs this, so add a short worked example after the box-net example.
Worked example: A kayaker is 4 km from the nearest point $A$ on a straight shore. She wants to reach, as soon as possible, a point $B$ on the shore a further 12 km from $A$.

She paddles at 6 km/h to a point on the shore $x$ km from $A$, then runs along the shore to $B$ at 10 km/h.

Find the landing point that minimises the time taken, and the minimum time.
1.
The distance paddled is $\sqrt{4^2+x^2}=\sqrt{16+x^2}$ km and the distance run is $(12-x)$ km. Using $\text{time}=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$T(x)=\frac{\sqrt{16+x^2}}{6}+\frac{12-x}{10}$$

2.
The landing point lies between $A$ and $B$.
$0\le x\le12$

3.
Find stationary points. By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{16+x^2}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{16+x^2}}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T'(x)&=\frac{x}{6\sqrt{16+x^2}}-\frac1{10}=0\\\frac{x}{6\sqrt{16+x^2}}&=\frac1{10}\\\color{#ef6068}{60\sqrt{16+x^2}\times}\,\frac{x}{6\sqrt{16+x^2}}&=\color{#ef6068}{60\sqrt{16+x^2}\times}\,\frac1{10}\\10x&=6\sqrt{16+x^2}\\5x&=3\sqrt{16+x^2}\\25x^2&=9(16+x^2)\quad\color{#ef6068}{(\text{squaring both sides})}\\16x^2&=144\\x^2&=9\\x&=3\quad(0\le x\le12)\end{aligned}$$
The root $x=-3$ is outside the domain. Check $x=3$ in $5x=3\sqrt{16+x^2}$: $15=3\times5$.
Checking minimum:
$$T''(x)=\frac{8}{3(16+x^2)^{3/2}}>0\quad\text{for all }x$$
The graph is concave up on the whole domain, so the stationary point at $x=3$ is the global minimum.

4.
She should land 3 km from $A$. The minimum time is $T(3)=\dfrac56+\dfrac9{10}=\dfrac{26}{15}$ hours, which is 1 hour 44 minutes.
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Solve each problem.
a) A bushwalker is 3 km from the nearest point $A$ on a straight road. She wants to reach, as soon as possible, a point $B$ on the road a further 10 km from $A$.

She walks through scrub at 4 km/h to a point on the road $x$ km from $A$, then walks along the road to $B$ at 5 km/h.

Find the value of $x$ that minimises the time taken, and the minimum time. (with a diagram)
b) A swimmer in difficulty is 40 m from a straight beach, directly out from a point $P$. A lifesaver on the beach is 120 m from $P$.

She runs along the beach at 5 m/s to a point $x$ m from her starting position, then swims straight to the swimmer at 3 m/s.

Find the value of $x$ that minimises the time taken, and the minimum time. (with a diagram)
Answers: a) $x=4$. The minimum time is $\dfrac{49}{20}=2.45$ hours.; b) $x=90$. The minimum time is $\dfrac{104}{3}\approx34.7$ seconds.
Comparison score: 59.

entries.description: Syllabus Content
MAV-12-06 applies calculus to graph functions and model and solve problems involving optimisation, rates of change and motion in a line
Optimisation
Define a global maximum of a function f(x) to be a point P(a, f(a)) on the graph where f(x) ≤ f(a), for all x in the domain, and define a global minimum similarly
Examine whether any discontinuities or endpoints of the domain on which f(x) is being considered are points of maxima or minima
Model optimisation problems in a variety of contexts by defining variables, noting domain restrictions if necessary, and establishing functions to represent the relationship between variables
Solve optimisation problems by using calculus to find local and global maxima and minima of differentiable functions, checking discontinuities of f′(x) and endpoints of the domain if applicable
Formulate conclusions to optimisation problems by evaluating solutions given the constraints of the domain

entries.description: Global Maxima and Minima

Mt Kosciuszko is the tallest mountain in Australia.
Mt Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.
Similarly, a turning point can be:
• A local maximum: the largest value in its neighbourhood.
• A global maximum: the largest value in its entire domain.
• A local minimum: the smallest value in its neighbourhood.
• A global minimum: the smallest value in its entire domain.

A neighbourhood in mathematics is
"the area immediately around a point"
(you will learn the formal definition in university)

To find global maxima and minima, examine and compare the function value f(x) at:
• Turning points.
• Domain boundaries.
• Discontinuities of f′(x).

entries.description:
Optimisation Problems
An optimisation problem involves finding the global maximum or minimum in a given domain.
1. Find f′(x).
2. Find stationary points in the domain and determine their nature using f″(x).
3. Find f(x) at the stationary points.
4. Check f(x) at endpoints of the domain.
5. State the maximum or minimum value of f(x).
Be mindful of units given by the question.

\(r^3=\frac{125}{\pi}\)
\(r=\frac{5}{\sqrt[3]{\pi}}\)
\(\frac{d^2S}{dr^2}=4\pi+\frac{1000}{r^3}\)

Supplied blue working: V = xyh; P = 2x + 2y = 40; x + y = 20; A = 2xy + 2xh + 2yh; 300 = 2xy + 2xh + 2yh; 150 = xy + xh + yh = xy + h(x + y) = xy + 20h. entries.description:
A landscape gardener wants to build a garden in the shape of a rectangle attached to a quarter-circle. Let x and y be the dimensions of the rectangle in metres, as shown in the diagram.

The garden bed is required to have an area of 36 m² and to have a perimeter which is as small as possible. Let P metres be the perimeter of the garden bed.
entries.presentation: Bold source identity above the question. Diagram between the opening paragraph and the area/perimeter conditions.

entries.description: Rectangle attached on its right to a quarter-circle. Rectangle height is labelled x beside its left edge; its top horizontal length is labelled y. The quarter-circle has radius x, with its centre at the rectangle’s bottom-right corner. Its arc joins the rectangle’s top-right corner to the right endpoint of the horizontal baseline. A dashed vertical radius marks the shared boundary. Right-angle markers appear at the rectangle’s top-left and bottom-left corners and between the dashed radius and the baseline extending right.
entries.presentation: Unshaded thin grey outlines; labels x and y in italic mathematical type. Rectangle and quarter-circle share a continuous horizontal baseline. Dimensions are not numerically specified.

entries.description: Show that P = 2x + 72/x
Find the smallest possible perimeter of the garden bed, showing why this is the minimum perimeter.

Area = xy + ¼πr²
36 = xy + ¼πx²
xy = 36 − πx²/4
y = 36/x − πx/4

∴ P = 2x + 2y + ¼(2πx)
= 2x + 2(36/x − πx/4) + πx/2
= 2x + 72/x − πx/2 + πx/2
= 2x + 72/x
entries.presentation: Supplied blue working in the left column beneath the question. Two separated derivation groups, with successive equality lines aligned. Teacher-answer content; exclude from student prompts.

entries.description:
P = 2x + 72/x
dP/dx = 2 − 72x⁻²
d²P/dx² = 144x⁻³

Max or min when dP/dx = 0:
2 − 72/x² = 0
2x² = 72
x² = 36
x = 6, (x > 0)

When x = 6,
d²P/dx² = 144/6³ = 2/3 > 0

⇒ MIN at x = 6

∴ P_min = 2 × 6 + 72/6
= 24 m
entries.expectedAnswer: The smallest possible perimeter is 24 m, attained at x = 6; the supplied second-derivative test establishes a minimum.
entries.presentation: Supplied blue working in the right column, alongside part a’s solution. Preserve derivative notation, grouped stages, implication arrow and final units. Teacher-answer content; exclude from student prompts.

entries.description: A cylinder of radius x and height 2h is to be inscribed in a sphere of radius R centred at O.

presentation.skillFocus: Optimisation of cylinder volume using differentiation

entries.description: Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by V = 2πh(R² − h²).
entries.expectedAnswer: Using Pythagoras, R² = h² + x², so x² = R² − h². Thus V = πx² × 2h = 2πh(R² − h²).

entries.description: Hence, or otherwise, show that the cylinder has a maximum volume when h = R/√3.
entries.expectedAnswer: h = R/√3; the supplied working establishes a maximum using the second derivative.

A vertical segment from O to the centre of the top rim is labelled h; a horizontal segment from that centre to the right rim is labelled x; the diagonal from O to the same right rim point is labelled R. A right-angle marker joins h and x at the top-rim centre.

presentation.position: Right of the question and its parts

entries.description: Supplied working: V = πr²h (general form); = πx² × 2h. Using Pythagoras: R² = h² + x²; x² = R² − h²; ∴ V = 2πh(R² − h²) … as required.

entries.description: Supplied working: V = 2πh(R² − h²) = 2πR²h − 2πh³; dV/dh = 2πR² − 3 × 2πh² = 2πR² − 6πh²; d²V/dh² = −12πh. Max or min when dV/dh = 0: 2πR² − 6πh² = 0; 6πh² = 2πR²; h² = R²/3; h = R/√3, h > 0. When h = R/√3, d²V/dh² = −12π × R/√3 < 0. ∴ Volume is a maximum when h = R/√3 units.

entries.description:
Show that the volume, V cm³, of the cone described above is given by
V = (⅓)πx²√(100 − x²)
Show that dV/dx = πx(200 − 3x²)/(3√(100 − x²)).
Find the exact value of θ for which V is a maximum.

Supplied blue working:
V = ⅓πr²h
Using Pythagoras,
h = √(100 − x²)
r = x
∴ Volume = ⅓πx²√(100 − x²)
entries.presentation: Answer-only content; upper left solution column.

entries.description:
Supplied blue working:
V = ⅓πx²√(100 − x²)
dV/dh = ⅓π[2x · √(100 − x²) − 2x · ½(100 − x²)^(−½) · x²]
= ⅓π[(2x(100 − x²) − x³)/√(100 − x²)]
= ⅓π[(200x − 2x³ − x³)/√(100 − x²)]
= πx(200 − 3x²)/(3√(100 − x²)) .. as required

entries.description:

Find x when dV/dx = 0

x = √(200/3)
When x < √(200/3), (200 − 3x²) > 0
⇒ dV/dx > 0
When x > √(200/3), (200 − 3x²) < 0

Equating the arc length of the section to the circumference of the cone:

10θ = 2π√(200/3)

entries.description:
HSC Advanced Sample Question Band 6
The figure shown represents a wire frame where ABCE is a convex quadrilateral.
The point D is on line segment EC with AB = ED = 2 cm and BC = a cm, where a is a positive constant.
Let ∠CBD = θ where 0 < θ < π/2.
entries.presentation: Bold question heading; diagram to the right of the question and its parts. Blue supplied solutions below are answer content only.

entries.description: Find BD and CD in terms of a and θ.
entries.expectedAnswer: BD = a cos θ; CD = a sin θ.

entries.description: Find the length, L cm, of the wire in the frame, including length BD, in terms of a and θ.
entries.expectedAnswer: L = 4 + a + 2a cos θ + a sin θ.

entries.description: Find dL/dθ, and hence show that dL/dθ = 0 when BD = 2CD.
entries.expectedAnswer: dL/dθ = −2a sin θ + a cos θ; setting this equal to zero gives a cos θ = 2a sin θ, hence BD = 2CD.

entries.description: Find the maximum value of L if a = 3√5.

Wire frame ABCE with A at bottom left, B above A, E at bottom right and C above E. D lies on EC level with B. Segments AB, BC, CE, EA and BD are drawn. AB and ED are each labelled 2 cm; BC is labelled a cm. Angle CBD is marked θ. Right-angle marks occur at A between AB and AE, at E between EA and EC, and at D between DB and DC.
entries.presentation: Black diagram. Rectangular ABDE beneath right triangle BDC; preserve vertex labels, internal wire BD, angle arc and all right-angle marks.

entries.description:
In ΔBCD,
cos θ = BD/a
∴ BD = a cos θ
sin θ = CD/a
∴ CD = a sin θ
entries.presentation: Blue supplied working in the left answer column.

entries.description:
L = 4 + 2BD + CD + a
= 4 + 2a cos θ + a sin θ + a
= 4 + a + 2a cos θ + a sin θ
entries.presentation: Blue supplied working; successive equality signs aligned.

entries.description:
Noting that a is a constant:
dL/dθ = −2a sin θ + a cos θ
When dL/dθ = 0,
−2a sin θ + a cos θ = 0
a cos θ = 2a sin θ
∴ BD = 2CD (using part (a))
entries.presentation: Blue supplied working in the left answer column.

entries.description:
SP’s when dL/dθ = 0,
−2a sin θ + a cos θ = 0
sin θ = ½ cos θ
tan θ = ½
If tan θ = ½, cos θ = 2/√5, sin θ = 1/√5
L_max = 4 + a + 2a cos θ + a sin θ
= 4 + (3√5) + 2(3√5)(2/√5) + (3√5)(1/√5)
= 4 + 3√5 + 12 + 3
= 19 + 3√5 cm
entries.presentation: Blue supplied working in the right answer column, with a reference triangle between the stationary-point calculation and trigonometric ratios.

entries.description:
Two circles have the same centre O.
The smaller circle has radius 1 cm, while the larger circle has radius (1 + x) cm.
The circles enclose a region QRST, which is subtended by an angle θ at O, as shaded.
The area of QRST is A cm², where A is a constant and A > 0.
Let P cm be the perimeter of QRST.
entries.presentation: Shared stem followed by parts a and b; annular-sector diagram beside the question.

entries.description: By finding expressions for the area and perimeter of QRST, show that P(x) = 2x + 2A/x.
Show that if the perimeter, P(x), is minimised, then θ must be less than 2.
entries.expectedAnswer: At the minimum, x² = A and θ = 2x/(x + 2) < 2.

entries.description: Two concentric circles centred at O. Two radial segments form an upward-facing sector. Q and R are the left and right outer-circle intersections; T and S are the corresponding inner-circle intersections. Shade the annular sector QRST. Label the left inner radial segment 1, its outer continuation x, and the angle between the radii at O with θ. Mark O with a point and its label.
entries.presentation: Whole circles visible; curved boundaries and radial sides define the shaded region. Diagram is to the right of the stem and parts. Dimensions uncertain.

entries.description:
Supplied working:
Area = Sector OQR − Sector OTS
A = θ/(2π) × π(1 + x)² − θ/(2π) × π × 1²
A = θ/2 (1 + x)² − θ/2
A = θ/2 (1 + 2x + x² − 1)
A = θ/2 x(x + 2)
θ = 2A/[x(x + 2)]

Perimeter QRST = θ/(2π) × 2π(x + 1) + θ/(2π) × 2π(1) + 2x
= θ(x + 1) + θ + 2x
= θ(x + 2) + 2x
= {2A/[x(x + 2)]}(x + 2) + 2x
= 2x + 2A/x
entries.presentation: Blue supplied solution in the lower left column. Preserve the area derivation followed by the perimeter derivation, with aligned continuation equalities. Answer content only.

entries.description:
Supplied working:
P(x) = 2x + 2A/x
P′(x) = 2 − 2A/x²
P″(x) = 4A/x³ > 0 (x, A > 0)
⇒ MIN when P′(x) = 0:
2 − 2A/x² = 0
2x² = 2A
x² = A

Using part (a):
θ = 2A/[x(x − 2)]
= 2x²/[x(x + 2)]
= 2x/(x + 2)
= 2 × x/(x + 2)
< 2 (since x/(x + 2) < 1 for all x)
∴ If P(x) is minimised, θ < 2.
entries.presentation: Blue supplied solution in the lower right column. Preserve the derivative test, implication arrow, substitution and inequality sequence. Answer content only.
